Subject: Scheduling approach for multi‑mode activities under resource and budget constraints

Team,

This memo outlines the scheduling challenge for our upcoming project. We are planning and sequencing a set of activities that share limited renewable resources and must be delivered within a fixed budget. Each activity can be executed in different ways (modes) that trade off speed, resource usage, and cost. Our task is to choose a single mode for each activity, set a feasible start date, and order activities so that we finish as early as possible without exceeding resource limits or the project budget.

Execution modes
- Each activity offers multiple execution options. Faster options shorten duration but require more resources and cost more; slower options take longer and generally cost less.
- Once an activity starts in a chosen mode, it runs without interruption until it completes. When it completes, the resources it was using become available for other work.

Dependencies and timing
- Certain activities must wait for others to finish before they can begin. Some of these relationships include a minimum wait (the successor cannot start until a specified time after the predecessor finishes). Others also include a maximum wait (the successor must start within a specified time window after the predecessor finishes).
- Some activities have earliest allowed start times that cannot be violated. If any activities have hard completion deadlines, those must also be respected.

Resources and conservative conflict management
- The project relies on multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity. To keep the plan safe and manageable, we apply a conservative sequencing rule for activities that are not connected by dependencies: if there exists even one combination of their execution modes and one resource type for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities cannot overlap in time. In that case, we must decide which one runs first and schedule them accordingly.
- This safety rule is the only resource control we apply; we do not perform any additional, continuous “sum of usages must stay within capacity at all times” check beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions.

Budget constraint
- Each mode choice carries a direct execution cost. The total cost across all chosen modes must remain within the fixed project budget. This means we must balance the desire for faster modes against overall spending limits.

Implications for planning
- Mode selection and activity ordering are tightly linked. Choosing faster modes can shorten the schedule but may exhaust the budget; choosing slower modes preserves budget but may lengthen the timeline.
- The minimum and maximum delay requirements between linked activities narrow the feasible windows for successors. Earliest start restrictions may leave unavoidable idle time. The conservative resource rule can force additional sequencing between otherwise independent activities, depending on how their potential modes interact.
- Together, these factors create a coordinated selection and sequencing challenge: we must pick one mode per activity, apply the dependency and timing rules, enforce the conservative resource sequencing, and remain under budget.

Goal
- Build a feasible schedule that minimizes the total project duration (makespan) while honoring all dependencies, timing requirements, resource safety rules, and the budget.

Next steps
- Confirm the activity list, mode data (durations, costs, and per‑resource requirements), resource capacities, dependencies with any minimum/maximum lags, earliest start dates, and any deadlines.
- Use these inputs to evaluate trade‑offs and produce a baseline plan that meets the budget and achieves the shortest feasible completion time.
